title: JavaScript
description: JavaScript is the language that brings web pages to life, letting you respond to clicks, change content, and build dynamic apps. Learn it step by step from variables to async code.

roadmap.title: Foundations
roadmap.blurb: Start here! Learn how to store data, make decisions, and repeat actions.

roadmap.title: Building Real Things
roadmap.blurb: Now work with collections of data and make web pages react to you.

topics.title: Variables & Types
topics.description: Learn how to store and label different kinds of data in JavaScript.

questions.question: Which keyword declares a variable whose value can be reassigned later?
questions.explanation: let declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned, while const cannot be reassigned.

questions.question: What is the data type of the value true in JavaScript?
questions.hint: It can only be true or false.
questions.explanation: Values that are only true or false are of the boolean type.

questions.question: Which of these is a string literal?
questions.explanation: Text wrapped in quotes like "hello" is a string. The others are a number, a boolean, and null.

questions.question: What does typeof undefined return?
questions.explanation: typeof undefined returns the string "undefined".

questions.question: What is the result of typeof null?
questions.hint: This is a famous JavaScript quirk.
questions.explanation: Due to a long-standing bug kept for compatibility, typeof null returns "object".

questions.question: Which declaration creates a constant that cannot be reassigned?
questions.hint: Its name hints at being unchangeable.
questions.explanation: const creates a binding that cannot be reassigned after its initial value.

questions.question: What keyword declares a block-scoped variable that you intend to reassign?
questions.explanation: let declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned.

questions.question: What operator do you use to check both value and type equality?
questions.explanation: The strict equality operator === compares value and type without coercion.

questions.question: What value does an uninitialized variable declared with let hold?
questions.explanation: A declared but unassigned variable holds the value undefined.

questions.question: What is the typeof result for the value 3.14 (give the string)?
questions.explanation: All numbers, including decimals, are of type "number" in JavaScript.

questions.question: Declare a constant named pi with the value 3.14 and log it to the console.
questions.code:
const pi = 3.14;
console.log(pi);
questions.explanation: const declares an unchangeable binding, and console.log prints its value.

questions.question: Create a variable name set to "Sam" and use a template literal to log "Hello, Sam!".
questions.code:
const name = "Sam";
console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);
questions.explanation: Template literals use backticks and ${} to embed variables inside strings.

questions.question: Convert the string "42" into a number and log the numeric result.
questions.hint: Number() converts a string to a number.
questions.explanation: Number() parses a numeric string and returns its number value, here 42.

questions.hint: x is undefined, and undefined + number is special.
questions.explanation: An uninitialized x is undefined; undefined coerced to a number is NaN, so undefined + 1 is NaN.

questions.question: Write code that logs true only if a variable score (a number) is both a number type and greater than 50.
questions.hint: Combine typeof and a comparison with &&.
questions.explanation: typeof checks the type and the && requires both conditions to be true before logging the boolean.

topics.title: Operators & Conditionals
topics.description: Learn to do math, compare values, and make your code take decisions.

questions.question: What does the operator % calculate?
questions.explanation: The modulo operator % returns the remainder after dividing one number by another.

questions.question: Which operator means 'logical AND'?
questions.explanation: && is the logical AND operator; both sides must be truthy for the result to be true.

questions.question: What does 5 > 3 evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Comparison operators return a boolean, and 5 is greater than 3, so the result is true.

questions.question: What is the difference between == and ===?
options: == compares value with type coercion, === compares value and type strictly
questions.explanation: == converts types before comparing (loose), while === compares both value and type without coercion (strict).

questions.question: What does the ternary expression age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor" return when age is 16?
questions.explanation: Because 16 is not >= 18, the condition is false and the value after the colon, "minor", is returned.

questions.question: Which value is considered falsy in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: The number 0 is falsy. The string "0", string "false", and an empty array are all truthy.

questions.question: What keyword starts a conditional block that runs when a condition is true?
questions.explanation: The if keyword begins a conditional block that runs when its condition is truthy.

questions.question: What single symbol is the logical NOT operator?
questions.explanation: The ! operator negates a boolean, turning true into false and vice versa.

questions.question: What does 10 % 3 evaluate to?
questions.explanation: 10 divided by 3 is 3 with a remainder of 1, so 10 % 3 is 1.

questions.question: What statement lets you choose among many cases based on one value?
questions.explanation: A switch statement compares a value against multiple case labels and runs the matching block.

questions.question: Write an if/else that logs "pass" if score is at least 60, otherwise logs "fail".
questions.explanation: The if checks the condition and runs the matching branch; here 72 >= 60 so it logs "pass".

questions.question: Use a ternary operator to set a variable label to "even" or "odd" based on the number n.
questions.explanation: The ternary checks if n divides evenly by 2; 7 leaves a remainder, so label becomes "odd".

questions.question: Write a switch statement on a variable day that logs "weekend" for "Sat" or "Sun" and "weekday" otherwise.
questions.hint: Stack the Sat and Sun cases, and use default.
questions.explanation: Stacking cases lets both "Sat" and "Sun" share a block, and default handles all other days.

questions.question:
What does the following log?
console.log(0 || "hi" && "bye");
questions.hint: && has higher precedence than ||, and evaluation stops at a truthy value.
questions.explanation: && runs first: "hi" && "bye" is "bye". Then 0 || "bye" returns the truthy "bye".

questions.question: Write a function classify(num) that returns "positive", "negative", or "zero" for any number.
questions.hint: Use if, else if, and else.
questions.explanation: The chained if/else if/else covers all three cases, returning the matching label for the sign of num.

topics.title: Loops & Functions
topics.description: Learn to repeat work with loops and package reusable logic into functions.

questions.question: Which keyword defines a traditional named function?
questions.hint: It is also the name of the concept.
questions.explanation: The function keyword declares a named function in JavaScript.

questions.question: What does a for loop's middle expression typically contain?
questions.hint: It decides whether to keep looping.
questions.explanation: A for loop is for (init; condition; step), and the middle part is the condition checked before each iteration.

questions.question: What keyword sends a value back out of a function?
questions.explanation: The return keyword passes a value back to whatever called the function and ends its execution.

questions.question: Which is a valid arrow function that doubles x?
questions.explanation: Arrow functions use the => syntax; const d = x => x * 2 implicitly returns x * 2.

questions.question: What does the break statement do inside a loop?
questions.explanation: break immediately stops the loop and continues with the code after it.

questions.question: What does continue do inside a loop?
questions.explanation: continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves on to the next one.

questions.question: What loop keyword repeats while a condition stays true and checks before each run?
questions.explanation: A while loop checks its condition before each iteration and repeats as long as it is true.

questions.question: What are the values passed into a function when you call it called?
questions.hint: They are the actual values, not the placeholders.
questions.explanation: Arguments are the actual values supplied to a function call, matching its parameters.

questions.question: What value does a function return if it has no return statement?
questions.hint: It is the default empty value.
questions.explanation: A function without a return statement implicitly returns undefined.

questions.question: What is the name for a function passed as an argument to another function?
questions.explanation: A callback is a function passed into another function to be called later.

questions.question: Write a function add(a, b) that returns the sum of a and b.
questions.explanation: The function returns the sum of its two parameters; add(2, 3) returns 5.

questions.question: Use a for loop to log the numbers 1 through 5.
questions.hint: Start at 1 and loop while i <= 5.
questions.explanation: The loop starts i at 1, continues while i <= 5, and increments i each time, logging 1 to 5.

questions.question: Write an arrow function isEven that returns true if a number is even.
questions.code:
const isEven = n => n % 2 === 0;
console.log(isEven(4));
questions.explanation: The arrow function implicitly returns the boolean result of n % 2 === 0; isEven(4) is true.

questions.hint: Watch the semicolon right after return.
questions.explanation: return; with nothing after it returns undefined, and the 5 line is never reached.

questions.question: Write a function factorial(n) that returns n! using a loop (factorial of 0 is 1).
questions.hint: Multiply numbers from 1 up to n into an accumulator.
questions.explanation: Starting result at 1 and multiplying by each integer up to n gives n!; factorial(5) is 120.

topics.title: Arrays & Objects
topics.description: Store lists and structured data, then transform them with built-in methods.

questions.question: How do you access the first element of an array named items?
questions.explanation: Array indexes start at 0, so items[0] is the first element.

questions.question: Which method adds an element to the end of an array?
questions.explanation: push() appends one or more elements to the end of an array.

questions.question: How do you read the property name from an object person?
questions.explanation: Object properties are accessed with dot notation like person.name, or bracket notation person["name"].

questions.question: What does array.map() return?
questions.hint: It produces something the same length.
options: The original array changed in place
A new array with each element transformed
questions.explanation: map() creates a new array of the same length where each element is the result of the callback.

questions.question: Which method keeps only elements that pass a test?
questions.explanation: filter() returns a new array containing only the elements for which the callback returns true.

questions.question: What does reduce() do?
options: Reduces an array to a single accumulated value
questions.explanation: reduce() runs a callback over each element, accumulating them into a single returned value.

questions.question: What property gives the number of elements in an array?
questions.explanation: The length property holds the number of elements in an array.

questions.question: What method removes and returns the last element of an array?
questions.explanation: pop() removes the last element of an array and returns it.

questions.question: What method returns an array of an object's keys (give the full call form, e.g. Object.xxx)?
questions.explanation: Object.keys(obj) returns an array of the object's own enumerable property names.

questions.question: What array method tests whether at least one element passes a condition?
questions.explanation: some() returns true if at least one element satisfies the callback test.

questions.question: Create an array of three colors and log its length.
questions.code:
const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];
console.log(colors.length);
questions.explanation: The array literal holds three strings, and .length reports 3.

questions.question: Use map() to create a new array of each number in nums doubled.
questions.explanation: map() applies the callback to each element, producing [2, 4, 6] without changing nums.

questions.question: Given an array nums, use filter() to keep only the even numbers.
questions.explanation: filter() keeps elements where the callback is true, producing [2, 4, 6].

questions.question: Use reduce() to compute the sum of all numbers in nums.
questions.hint: Start the accumulator at 0 and add each value.
questions.explanation: reduce() accumulates each element into sum starting from 0, yielding 60.
b and a reference the same array, so pushing through b also changes a; its length becomes 4.

questions.question: Given an object person with name and age, log each key and value using Object.entries and a for...of loop.
questions.explanation: Object.entries returns key/value pairs, and destructuring in the for...of loop logs each pair.

topics.title: DOM & Events
topics.description: Select page elements, change them, and respond to user actions like clicks.

questions.question: What does DOM stand for?
questions.explanation: DOM stands for Document Object Model, the tree structure representing a web page.

questions.question: Which method selects a single element by its id?
questions.explanation: document.getElementById returns the element with the matching id, or null if none exists.

questions.question: Which method selects the first element matching a CSS selector?
questions.hint: It uses a query and a selector.
questions.explanation: document.querySelector returns the first element matching the given CSS selector.

questions.question: Which method attaches a click handler to an element btn?
questions.hint: You add a listener for an event.
questions.explanation: addEventListener("click", handler) registers a function to run when the element is clicked.

questions.question: What property changes the text content of an element?
questions.hint: It refers to the text inside.
questions.explanation: textContent gets or sets the plain text inside an element.

questions.question: Inside an event handler, what does event.preventDefault() do?
questions.hint: It stops the browser's normal reaction.
questions.explanation: preventDefault() cancels the browser's default behavior, such as submitting a form or following a link.

questions.question: What method selects ALL elements matching a CSS selector?
questions.explanation: document.querySelectorAll returns a NodeList of all elements matching the selector.

questions.question: What property holds the current text typed into an input field?
questions.explanation: The value property of an input element holds the current text entered by the user.

questions.question: What object property in a click handler refers to the element that was clicked?
questions.explanation: event.target refers to the element that triggered the event.

questions.question: What property of an element lets you add or remove CSS classes via add() and remove()?
questions.hint: It is a list of classes.
questions.explanation: The classList property exposes add, remove, toggle, and contains for managing an element's CSS classes.

questions.question: Select the element with id "title" and change its text to "Welcome".
questions.code:
const title = document.getElementById("title");
title.textContent = "Welcome";
questions.explanation: getElementById finds the element, and assigning to textContent replaces its text.

questions.question: Add a click listener to the button with id "go" that logs "clicked" when pressed.
questions.explanation: addEventListener registers the arrow function to run on every click of the button.

questions.question: Create a new li element with text "Item" and append it to the ul with id "list".
questions.explanation: createElement builds a new node, textContent sets its text, and appendChild adds it to the list.

questions.question: Attach a submit handler to a form with id "form" that prevents the default action and logs the input's value (input id "name").
questions.hint: Use preventDefault and read the input value.
questions.explanation: preventDefault stops the page from reloading, and we read the entered text from the input's value.

questions.question: You add one click listener to a parent ul and check event.target to handle clicks on its li children. What pattern is this?
questions.hint: The event bubbles up to the parent.
questions.explanation: Event delegation uses a single listener on a parent and inspects event.target to handle events from many children, leveraging bubbling.

topics.title: ES6+ & Async Basics
topics.description: Use modern syntax like destructuring and spread, plus promises and async/await.

questions.question: What does the spread operator ... do with an array?
questions.explanation: The spread operator expands an array's elements, useful for copying or combining arrays.

questions.question: Which syntax pulls properties out of an object into variables?
questions.explanation: Destructuring extracts values from objects or arrays into distinct variables.

questions.question: What does an async function always return?
questions.explanation: An async function always returns a Promise, even if its body returns a plain value.

questions.question: What keyword pauses an async function until a Promise settles?
questions.explanation: await pauses an async function until the awaited Promise resolves or rejects.

questions.question: What method handles a rejected Promise?
questions.explanation: .catch() registers a handler that runs when a Promise rejects with an error.

questions.question: What does the default parameter in function greet(name = "friend") do?
questions.hint: It fills in when nothing is passed.
options: Throws an error if name is missing
questions.explanation: A default parameter supplies its value only when the argument is missing or undefined.

questions.question: What keyword marks a function so it can use await inside it?
questions.explanation: The async keyword marks a function as asynchronous, allowing await inside it.

questions.question: What three-dot symbol is used for both spread and rest?
questions.hint: It is three of the same character.
questions.explanation: The ... token serves as the spread operator (expanding) and the rest operator (collecting).

questions.question: What Promise method runs whether it resolves or rejects?
questions.hint: It always happens at the end.
questions.explanation: .finally() runs its callback after a Promise settles, regardless of success or failure.

questions.question: What is the modern browser API function used to make HTTP requests (one word)?
questions.hint: It is the function name itself.
questions.explanation: fetch() is the modern browser API that returns a Promise for making network requests.

questions.question: Use destructuring to pull name and age out of the object user.
questions.explanation: Object destructuring assigns user.name to name and user.age to age in one statement.

questions.question: Use the spread operator to merge arrays a and b into one array.
questions.hint: Put both inside a new array literal with ...
questions.explanation: Spreading both arrays into a new literal produces [1, 2, 3, 4] without mutating the originals.

questions.question: Write an async function getData that awaits fetch on a url and returns the parsed JSON.
questions.explanation: await pauses for the fetch Promise, then for response.json(), returning the parsed data from the async function.

questions.question: Write a function sum that uses rest parameters to add any number of arguments.
questions.explanation: The rest parameter collects all arguments into an array, and reduce sums them; sum(1,2,3,4) is 10.

questions.hint: Synchronous code first, then microtasks (promises) before macrotasks (timers).
questions.explanation: Synchronous A and D run first; the Promise microtask C runs before the setTimeout macrotask B, giving A D C B.
